title: Python's int("\u0663") is 3; JavaScript's Number("\u0663") is NaN
assumption: A "digits only" check (\d or isdigit) and a numeric parser agree on what counts as a digit, and that agreement is the same in every language.

input.description: A quantity, price, or phone-number field filled in using a non-Latin numeral system that is still, by Unicode's own definition, a decimal digit.

what_goes_wrong: In Python, "\u0663".isdigit() is True, "\u0663".isdecimal() is True, int("\u0663") == 3, and a bare regex r"\d" matches it. In JavaScript, the ASCII-only /\d/ regex does NOT match it, and both Number("\u0663") and parseInt("\u0663", 10) return NaN — the identical character is "a valid number" in one language's standard library and "not a number at all" in the other's.
why: ARABIC-INDIC DIGIT THREE has General_Category Nd and Numeric_Type=Decimal, exactly like ASCII "3": it is a real decimal digit in its own numeral system. Python's int() accepts strings made of any Unicode decimal digits (category Nd), so int("\u0663") is 3 and int("\u0663\u0661") is 31, and the re module's \d matches any Nd character for str patterns unless re.ASCII is set. In JavaScript, \d is defined as exactly [0-9], with or without the u or v flag, and Number()/parseInt() only accept ASCII digits in their string grammar, so the same character is rejected.

repros.code:
import re
s = "\u0663"
print(s.isdigit(), s.isdecimal())
print(int(s), int(s) == 3)
print(re.match(r"^\d+$", s) is not None)

fix: If you intend "ASCII digits only", say so explicitly (Python: re.match(r"\d+", s, re.ASCII); JavaScript's \d already is ASCII-only). If you intend to accept any script's digits, normalize non-ASCII decimal digits to ASCII before further processing (Python's unicodedata.decimal() per character, or NFKC for digits that have compatibility decompositions) rather than relying on int()/Number() to agree across languages — they don't.

sources.title: ECMAScript spec: ToNumber applied to the String type

test_cases.note: A "digits only" validator should either accept this consistently in both Python and JS or reject it consistently in both — not one and not the other, by accident of which language's \d it used.
